top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: We followed the methods suggested in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-­ Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. 28 In accordance with the guidelines, our systematic review/meta-­ analysis protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews on 11 July 2022 and was last updated on 19 January 2023 (registration number CRD42022343383).

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: A total of eight cross-­ sectional studies were included in the meta-­ analysis. We identified 3775 articles by searching the databases MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (Ovid) and Web of Science. A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools. Another 546 studies were removed for additional reasons. We examined the titles and abstracts of 208 studies and excluded 157 on the basis of our findings. We screened 51 articles for eligibility. Eight studies were included in the meta-­ analysis. The PRISMA flow chart is shown in figure 1.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: - ⇒ This is the first systematic review and meta-­ analysis exclusively focused on the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS in children and adolescents. - ⇒ Low adherence to the MedDiet is significantly associated with increased odds of having MetS among youth (odds ratio [OR] = 2.18; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.45 to 3.28). - ⇒ The findings were consistent across diverse countries and dietary assessment tools, despite moderate heterogeneity.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Background The Mediterranean diet has been associated with improved metabolic health among adults. This meta-­ analysis aimed to evaluate the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents. Methods A systematic review of the literature was conducted by searching PubMed, the Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus and Web of Science, covering publications from inception to April 2024. Studies were included if they evaluated the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents. A random-­ effects model was used to estimate the summary effect size. Results A total of eight studies involving children and adolescents aged 6 to 19 years were included in the meta-­ analysis (n=6562, 50% girls). Low adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome than was medium/high adherence (odds ratio [OR] = 2.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.45 to 3.28; p < 0.001; inconsistency index [ I 2 ] = 64.15%). Conclusion This meta-­ analysis suggested that increased adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with lower probabilities of having cardiometabolic risk among children and adolescents. Thus, our findings suggest that public health strategies are needed to implement and promote effective actions toward healthy eating habits in children and adolescents.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Two authors independently conducted systematic searches in the following databases: Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed. The searches included studies published from database inception to 22 April 2024. The search was limited to peer-­ reviewed studies published in English. A professional librarian was consulted to ensure the quality of the search strategy.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross-­ sectional study design. However, to narrow the scope of the meta-­ analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included. In contrast, the exclusion criteria included adults and adolescents/children with evidence of metabolic or autoimmune liver disease, diabetes or the presence of known systemic disease. Studies were also excluded if they presented duplicate data from the same source and year. When two studies used duplicate data from the same source and year, the study with the larger sample size was selected.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: The characteristics of the eight studies included in this meta-­ analysis are presented in table 2. All studies were cross-­ sectional in design and published between 2011 and 2022. The studies were conducted in diverse geographic settings, including Europe (Spain, Greece, Italy), the Middle East (Iran), the USA and Turkey. The sample sizes ranged from 137 to 1972 participants, with the proportion of female participants ranging from 47.5% to 60.5%. Figure 1 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-­ Analyses flowchart. There was considerable heterogeneity in the age of participants across studies, ranging from 6 to 19 years, covering both early and late adolescence. Dietary adherence to the MedDiet was assessed via different tools: five studies employed the KIDMED index, whereas three used FFQs to derive MedDiet scores or patterns. The KIDMED is a validated, structured index specifically designed to measure adherence to the MedDiet in young populations and is based on a 16-­ item scoring system. In contrast, FFQs are broader tools used to assess usual dietary intake, from which MedDiet adherence scores are derived using predefined criteria. Similarly, outcome measures varied, with most studies using International Diabetes Federation (IDF) criteria for defining MetS, while some also included definitions based on homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-­ IR) or other phenotype-­ based approaches (eg, metabolically unhealthy obesity [MUO]). The main results consistently indicated an inverse association between adherence to the MedDiet and the presence of MetS or its components, although FFQ, food frequency questionnaire; HOMA-­ IR, Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance; top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: A search strategy was used to identify all eligible studies published before 22 April 2024. The search strategy included controlled vocabulary terms specific to each database along with keywords derived from scoping index articles relevant to this meta-­ analysis. The following terms related to the MedDiet were used: MEDdiet, Mediterranean Diet Quality Index for Children and Adolescents (KIDMED) score, MedDiet score, MedDiet and hypertension, MedDiet and diabetes, KIDMED and MedDiet score. The following outcome terms related to MetS were included: MetS or components (hyperlipidaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia, hypertension) combined with health. The reference lists of eligible studies were manually examined to find further relevant papers and included if suitable. Any disagreements were settled through consensus with a third author. The complete search strategies used for all the databases are presented in online supplemental file 2.
